introduction-the-end-of-the-maintenance-.core: Modern deployment strategies release without downtime by running old and new versions side by side and controlling which traffic reaches which, so a release is reversible and low-risk.

first_principles.problem: Saturday-night maintenance windows mean downtime, big-bang risk and painful rollbacks.
truths: Running versions side by side makes switching possible.
derivation: **Blue/green**: switch all at once and switch back.
**Shadow**: mirror traffic with no user impact.

analogy.title: Renovating a restaurant while staying open
analogy.story: Redo one section at a time, or open a twin restaurant next door and move diners over.
analogy.breaks: Zero-downtime deploys still need backward-compatible schemas and APIs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Releases happen on a Tuesday afternoon, safely.

check.a: Running old and new versions simultaneously and controlling traffic between them.

rolling-updates-the-slow-and-steady-repl.core: A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time (controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable) and waits for readiness before continuing. It's the Kubernetes default: simple and cheap, but rollback is gradual and both versions serve at once.

first_principles.problem: You need to update 20 pods without downtime or doubling capacity.
truths: Capacity must stay sufficient during the update.
New instances must be healthy before they take traffic.
derivation: **maxSurge**: extra pods allowed; **maxUnavailable**: pods allowed down.
Pause or undo if things go wrong.

analogy.title: Changing tyres on a moving car, one at a time
analogy.story: The car keeps rolling because the other three tyres carry it.
analogy.breaks: Both versions serve at once, so they must be compatible. Rollback is another rolling update.

code.text:
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 25%
    maxUnavailable: 0

check.a: Capacity never drops below the desired replica count during the update.

bluegreen-deployment-the-instant-switch.core: Run two complete environments. Blue serves production while green gets the new version and is tested. Then the router flips all traffic to green at once, and switching back is just as instant.

first_principles.problem: You need an instant cut-over and an instant rollback, with no mixed versions serving users.
truths: A full parallel environment can be verified before any users touch it.
Keeping the old environment allows instant reversal.
derivation: **Switch** the load balancer or service selector.

analogy.title: A light switch between two rooms
analogy.story: Flip it and the whole house is lit by the new room; flip it back if the bulb flickers.
analogy.breaks: It doubles infrastructure cost, and database changes must work for both versions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 100% of traffic moves in seconds, and rollback takes seconds too.

code.text:
kubectl patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api","color":"green"}}}'
# rollback: color: blue

check.a: Running two full production environments at the same time.

canary-deployment-testing-the-waters.core: Release the new version to a small slice of real traffic (1–5%), compare its metrics with the baseline, and increase step by step, or roll back automatically if errors or latency get worse.

first_principles.problem: Some bugs only appear under real production traffic, and exposing everyone at once maximises the blast radius.
derivation: **Compare** error rate and latency against the baseline.

analogy.title: A canary in the coal mine
analogy.story: The small bird shows danger early, before the miners are affected.
analogy.breaks: Low traffic means weak statistics, and some bugs only appear at scale.

example.title: An automated canary

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: When the 5xx rate rises at 5%, it rolls back with 95% of users untouched.

example.outcome: real-traffic validation with limited blast radius.

check.q: Why compare canary metrics against a baseline?
check.a: So you measure the new version's effect, not general traffic fluctuations.

shadow-deployment-the-stealth-mode.core: Mirror copies of real production requests to the new version, whose responses are discarded. You test it with real load and real request shapes, with zero user impact.

first_principles.problem: You want to know how a rewritten service handles real traffic before any user depends on it.
truths: Side effects in the mirror can still cause harm.
derivation: **Mirror** traffic at the proxy or mesh (Istio, Envoy).

analogy.title: A trainee pilot in a simulator fed by real flight data
analogy.story: They fly the real route in parallel, but their controls don't move the actual plane.
analogy.breaks: Writes and side effects must be isolated, or the shadow double-charges customers.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: v2's p99 is 3x higher on long queries, so it's fixed before any user sees it.

check.q: What's the main danger of shadow deployments?
check.a: Side effects such as writes, payments or emails being executed twice by the shadow service.

choosing-the-right-strategy-a-decision-f.core: Choose a strategy by risk, cost and need: rolling for routine low-risk changes, blue/green for instant all-or-nothing switches, canary for risky changes validated on real traffic, and shadow for rewrites or performance validation.

first_principles.problem: Using one strategy for everything either wastes money or takes unnecessary risk.
truths: Strategies differ in cost and complexity.
Rollback speed matters differently per change.
derivation: **Rewrite or performance unknown** → shadow, then canary.

analogy.title: Choosing transport for a trip
analogy.story: Walk to the corner shop, drive across town, take a test drive before buying a car.
analogy.breaks: Strategies combine. For example, shadow, then canary, then a full rollout.

example.title: Three releases this week
flow: Search engine rewrite → shadow, then canary

steps.label: Principle
steps.detail: Match the strategy to the risk.

check.q: Which strategy suits a performance-critical rewrite?
check.a: Shadow (to validate under real load safely), followed by a canary.

deployment-strategies-in-the-real-world-.core: Production teams automate strategies with controllers (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker) that shift traffic through meshes or ingress, run metric analysis against Prometheus or Datadog, and promote or abort without humans.

first_principles.problem: Manually adjusting traffic weights and watching dashboards is slow, error-prone and doesn't scale to many services.
derivation: Declare the rollout **steps** as a CRD.

analogy.title: An autopilot with automatic abort
analogy.story: The plane follows the approach and goes around automatically if the instruments show danger.
analogy.breaks: Bad metrics give bad decisions, so choose meaningful SLIs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A rollout below 99% success aborts automatically.

code.text:
metrics:
- name: success-rate
  successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99
  provider:
    prometheus:
      query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api",code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api"}[5m]))

check.q: What does an AnalysisTemplate do in Argo Rollouts?
check.a: It defines metric queries and success conditions that gate promotion or trigger an abort.
